notes:
All supplied details confirmed. Crossref (DOI 10.1093/restud/rdy065) gives RESTUD 86(5):1867–1900; print issue October 2019, published online 16 November 2018. Prior-title claim confirmed: arXiv:1312.7614v1 (30 Dec 2013) is titled "Testing many moment inequalities"; the arXiv listing was retitled by v5/v6 (30 Sep / 18 Oct 2018) to "Inference on causal and structural parameters using many moment inequalities" (arXiv uses sentence case; the journal uses title case). Six arXiv versions: v1 2013-12-30, v2 2014-06-03, v3 2014-06-22, v4 2014-11-21, v5 2018-09-30, v6 2018-10-18. Also circulated as cemmap working paper CWP52/14.

EXTRA QUESTION — Theorem 4.3 and Comment 4.6. Both exist, in Section 4 ("Critical values"). Verified by extracting full text from two independent copies of the accepted version: arXiv:1312.7614v6 PDF and the author-hosted PDF at https://denischetverikov.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/moment_ineq_v27.pdf — both put "4. Critical values" as the section head, Theorem 4.3 and Comment 4.6 at the same positions.

Theorem 4.3 is headed "(Validity of one-step MB and EB methods)". Precisely: let c_B(alpha) denote either c_MB(alpha) (multiplier bootstrap) or c_EB(alpha) (empirical bootstrap); assume constants 0 < c1 < 1/2 and C1 > 0 with (M_{n,3}^2 v M_{n,4}^2 v B_n)^2 log^{7/2}(pn) <= C1 n^{1/2-c1}  [eq. (35)]. Then there exist positive c, C depending only on c1, C1 such that under H0, P(T > c_B(alpha)) <= alpha + C n^{-c}  [eq. (36)]; and in addition, if mu_j = 0 for all 1 <= j <= p, then |P(T > c_B(alpha)) - alpha| <= C n^{-c}  [eq. (37)]. Both bounds hold uniformly over all distributions L_X satisfying (12) and (35). So a nuance worth flagging: Theorem 4.3 is *stated* as a bootstrap-critical-value validity result for T = max of p Studentized statistics, not as a CLT; it is Comment 4.6 that gives the CLT reading.

Comment 4.6 is headed "(High dimension bootstrap CLT)" and says: the result (37) can be understood as a high dimensional bootstrap CLT for maxima of studentized sample averages. It shows such maxima can be approximated either by multiplier or empirical bootstrap methods even if maxima are taken over (very) many sample averages; the distributional approximation holds with polynomially (in n) small error. It states this result complements a high dimensional bootstrap CLT for NON-studentized sample averages derived in Chernozhukov, Chetverikov and Kato (2013) [Ann. Statist., Gaussian approximations and multiplier bootstrap] and (2017) [Ann. Probab., Central limit theorems and bootstrap in high dimensions], and may be of interest in many other settings, well beyond the problem of testing many moment inequalities.

Section 4 contents for reference: Theorems 4.1 (one-step SN), 4.2 (two-step SN), 4.3 (one-step MB/EB), 4.4 (two-step MB/EB), 4.5 (hybrid two-step), 4.6 (three-step MB/EB); Comments 4.1–4.11.

query: Kish — "Survey Sampling", John Wiley & Sons, 1965 (book). Confirm the publisher, year and that Kish introduced the term "design effect".
venue_exact: John Wiley & Sons, Inc., New York (Wiley Series in Probability and Mathematical Statistics), 1965, xvi + 643 pp.
notes: PUBLISHER AND YEAR CONFIRMED: Leslie Kish, Survey Sampling, John Wiley & Sons, Inc., New York, 1965. Verified via the Open Library catalogue record (OL5947497M: J. Wiley, New York, 1965, xvi + 643 p., LCCN 65019479, OCLC 256017); corroborated by the 1966 review in the American Political Science Review, Cambridge Core ("New York: John Wiley & Sons, Inc., 1965. Pp. xvi, 643") and by the 1968 Biometrische Zeitschrift review (DOI 10.1002/bimj.19680100122), which gives "John Wiley & Sons, Inc., New York, London 1965, IX + 643 S." — note the two reviews disagree on the front-matter pagination (xvi vs IX); the catalogue records use xvi. The book was reissued unchanged in 1995 in the Wiley Classics Library (ISBN 978-0-471-10949-5), so some citations show 1995 — cite 1965 for the original. DESIGN EFFECT CONFIRMED: Kish coined the term "design effect" (deff) in this 1965 book, where he gave the general definition (variance under the actual design divided by the variance under simple random sampling of the same size), the cluster-sampling form deff = 1 + (m-1)*rho involving the intraclass correlation, and the unequal-weighting form deff = n * sum(w_i^2) / (sum(w_i))^2 — the last is universally called "Kish's design effect" or the "Kish factor"; relevant pages are pp. 88, 162, 258 and 427. Attribution verified on the Wikipedia and HandWiki "Design effect" articles (history sections), and the formula attribution to Kish (1965) is repeated in the CRAN PracTools "Design Effects and Effective Sample Size" vignette. Precursors exist but do not use the name: the 19th-century "Lexis ratio" and Cornfield (1951), both noted by Kish himself in his later review "Methods for Design Effects", Journal of Official Statistics 11(1), 1995, pp. 55-77; Kish's earlier "Confidence Intervals for Clustered Samples", American Sociological Review 22(2), 1957, pp. 154-165, works with the same variance ratio for clustered samples but the term "design effect" itself is standardly credited to the 1965 book. No DOI or arXiv id (pre-DOI monograph); WorldCat record is OCLC 256017 (https://search.worldcat.org/oclc/256017), which returned HTTP 429 on direct fetch, so the metadata above rests on Open Library plus the two contemporaneous published reviews.
